claims.claim: Palmatier says Kay alters the familiar world at the level of everyday ritual, myth, legend and superstition rather than by cosmetic changes.
claims.source: Joshua Palmatier (novelist), 'Altering the Familiar: Tigana by Guy Gavriel Kay', Reactor/Tor.com 'That Was Awesome! Writers on Writing', 2016
claims.quote: down to arbitrary everyday rituals, including myths and legends and superstitions
claims.page: body, paragraph beginning 'How he does is it arcane'

claims.claim: Mather says Kay's poetic style is not so dense that passages require hours of thought to decipher.
claims.source: Andrew Mather, 'The Masters Of Prose', The Quill to Live (review blog), 2016
claims.quote: incredibly poetic but also not too dense

claims.claim: Mather calls Kay the most transportive writer he has read, attributing it to years of study of the cultures and places written about.
claims.source: Andrew Mather, 'The Masters Of Prose', The Quill to Live (review blog), 2016
claims.quote: Kay is the most transportive writer I have ever read

claims.claim: Michal says The Last Light of the Sun cuts Kay's ornate style down to a rougher language full of sentence fragments.
claims.source: Michal, 'Flippant Reviews: Guy Gavriel Kay', One Last Sketch (blog), 2011
claims.quote: rife with sentence fragments and strong images recounting the frozen north
claims.page: entry for The Last Light of the Sun

claims.claim: Michal says The Last Light of the Sun has one of the most beautiful closing sentences he has encountered anywhere.
claims.source: Michal, 'Flippant Reviews: Guy Gavriel Kay', One Last Sketch (blog), 2011
claims.quote: one of the most beautiful closing sentences I’ve encountered anywhere
claims.page: entry for The Last Light of the Sun

claims.claim: Michal faults Tigana for telling the reader how to feel rather than leaving the feeling to be inferred.
claims.source: Michal, 'Flippant Reviews: Guy Gavriel Kay', One Last Sketch (blog), 2011
claims.quote: We’re all too often told how to feel

claims.claim: Michal names as a flaw Kay's tendency to digress into long passages describing the vast import of a historical moment.
claims.source: Michal, 'Flippant Reviews: Guy Gavriel Kay', One Last Sketch (blog), 2011
claims.quote: off on long tangents describing the vast import of some historical moment

claims.claim: Kay states in his own essay that there are no rules for writing, offering his own practice as anecdote rather than prescription.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, 'Some Writing Advice: Don't Take Others' Advice', Literary Hub, 2019
claims.page: body, paragraph beginning 'There are no rules'

claims.feature: other: sentence-level craft as a value
claims.claim: Kay names sentence-by-sentence insight and brilliance in Shirley Hazzard's The Transit of Venus as the object of his extreme admiration.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, '5 Books in My Life', Literary Hub, 2016
claims.quote: the sentence by sentence insight and brilliance is extreme
claims.page: answer to 'Is there a book you wish you had written?'

claims.claim: Kay says he does not write like Shirley Hazzard even though he admires her craft.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, '5 Books in My Life', Literary Hub, 2016
claims.page: answer to 'Is there a book you wish you had written?'

claims.claim: Kay says the books he rereads most are the poetry of Yeats or George Seferis.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, '5 Books in My Life', Literary Hub, 2016
claims.quote: the poetry of Yeats or George Seferis
claims.page: answer to 'What's the book you reread the most?'

claims.claim: Kay says it is important to him that readers who know nothing of the actual history never feel behind the curve.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, quoted from a Morrin Centre talk by Joel Miller, 'I Drove 12 Hours to Meet Guy Gavriel Kay', Transmissions from Tomorrow (Substack), 2026
claims.quote: don’t ever feel they’re behind the curve or missing something
claims.page: section 'You Don't Need a Course in the 100 Years War'

claims.claim: Kay says he has no pattern, template or system for writing a novel.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, quoted from a Morrin Centre talk by Joel Miller, 'I Drove 12 Hours to Meet Guy Gavriel Kay', Transmissions from Tomorrow (Substack), 2026
claims.quote: I don’t have a pattern, a template, or a system
claims.page: section 'On Craft: There Is No System'

claims.claim: Kay says writing characters who are aware of their own past and their country's and culture's past is what lets him work with historical awareness.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, quoted from a Morrin Centre talk by Joel Miller, 'I Drove 12 Hours to Meet Guy Gavriel Kay', Transmissions from Tomorrow (Substack), 2026
claims.quote: aware of their own past and the past of their country

claims.claim: A reader commenting on the piece describes Kay's writing as seeming casual yet perfect.
claims.source: David McMillan, reader comment on Joel Miller's 'I Drove 12 Hours to Meet Guy Gavriel Kay', Transmissions from Tomorrow (Substack), 2026
claims.quote: it seems so casual yet so perfect
